overview:
Pakistan stretches from the Arabian Sea north into some of the highest mountains on Earth, bordering India, China, Afghanistan and Iran. It covers about 880,000 km², roughly twice the size of California, and the Indus River runs almost its whole length, feeding one of the world's largest irrigation systems.

About 240 million people live in Pakistan, making it the fifth most populous country in the world. Urdu and English are the official languages, while Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Saraiki and Balochi are spoken at home by tens of millions. Islamabad, built in the 1960s below the Margalla Hills, is the capital; Karachi on the coast and Lahore in the east are far larger cities.

Pakistan is a federal parliamentary republic and the world's second most populous Muslim-majority country. It is known for cricket, for the ancient cities of the Indus Valley, and for the Karakoram peaks that draw climbers from everywhere.
landAndNature: Three great mountain ranges meet in northern Pakistan: the Himalaya, Karakoram and Hindu Kush. K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world and among the deadliest to climb, stands in the Karakoram, along with glaciers such as the Baltoro that are among the longest outside the polar regions. South of the mountains spread the fertile plains of Punjab, watered by five rivers whose name means exactly that. The Thar Desert covers the southeast, and the dry Balochistan plateau the west. Snow leopards, markhor goats with corkscrew horns, and Himalayan brown bears live in the high country; the Indus River dolphin, nearly blind and found nowhere else, swims in the murky river below.
peopleAndCulture: Pakistani food is famous for its spice and variety: biryani rice, nihari stew simmered overnight, chapli kebabs, naan from clay ovens, and mangoes so good that summer is planned around them. Qawwali, a hypnotic devotional singing style built on hand claps and harmonium, was carried worldwide by Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan. Cricket is a national obsession, and Pakistan won the World Cup in 1992; squash players from one Pakistani family dominated the sport for decades. Truck art turns cargo trucks into rolling paintings covered in flowers, poetry and mirrors. Eid festivals bring feasts and new clothes, and Basant in Lahore once filled the sky with kites. Malala Yousafzai, shot for insisting girls attend school, became the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner in 2014.
history: One of the world's first urban civilizations grew here: the Indus Valley cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa had brick drains, public baths and planned streets around 2500 BC. Persians, Alexander the Great, the Maurya emperors and the Buddhist kingdom of Gandhara all left their mark. Islam arrived in Sindh in the 700s, and the Mughal emperors built Lahore's fort and mosques. Britain ruled the whole subcontinent from the 1800s. In 1947 British India was partitioned into India and Pakistan; about 15 million people fled across the new borders and hundreds of thousands were killed in the violence. East Pakistan broke away in 1971 to become Bangladesh. The mountainous region of Kashmir is claimed by both India and Pakistan and divided between them, and has been fought over since 1947.
funFacts: Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BC, had covered sewers and a great public bath long before ancient Rome existed.
The Karakoram Highway to China is one of the highest paved international roads in the world, crossing a pass near 4,700 meters.
Pakistan has five of the world's fourteen mountains above 8,000 meters, including K2.
Pakistani truck drivers spend a fortune decorating their vehicles with hand-painted flowers, portraits, poetry and jangling chains.
More than half of the world's hand-stitched soccer balls, including World Cup balls, are made in the city of Sialkot.
